According to Mark Gurman's latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering making several changes to its App Store. The goal? To increase the potential revenue it generates.

Apple's specific plans for changes to the App Store are not yet clear. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to increase profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," and this effort is being primarily driven by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

This effort is reportedly part of the reason longtime veteran Phil Schiller left the company last week. Schiller transitioned to the role of Apple Fellow after stepping down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020, and part of his responsibilities included overseeing the App Store. Schiller is not a fan of this idea:

Apple has a lot of ways it could increase the App Store's profit margins. It could eliminate the existing human app review process—a process that is costly, though may not be as effective in the age of agentic coding. However, people probably wouldn't be thrilled about further automating reviews, even though doing so would certainly help cut costs.

It could also raise the fees for developer memberships, which currently stand at $99 per year. Considering that many small developers spend $200 per month on subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, you could easily argue Apple has reason to raise prices and developers would still pay up. The company could also charge subscription fees to large developers based on traffic, passing on some of the infrastructure costs.

How it all plays out, only time will tell, but I'm quite curious to see what these changes will actually become.
